dimensions.summary: The OG-Deut translator occupies a middle position on the literalness spectrum—more literal than OG-Isaiah but less isomorphic than the kaige-Theodotionic tradition. In Deut 18:15, the rendering is quite close: נָבִיא = προφήτην, כָּמֹנִי = ὡς ἐμέ, יָקִים = ἀναστήσει, אֵלָיו תִּשְׁמָעוּן = αὐτοῦ ἀκούσεσθε, preserving word order closely. However, the expansions in 32:43 (adding οὐρανοί, υἱοὶ θεοῦ, ἄγγελοι θεοῦ lines) and the divergence in 32:8 (בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל rendered ἀγγέλων θεοῦ, likely reflecting a different Vorlage or an interpretive tradition) show that formal equivalence is not the translator's absolute governing principle. Aejmelaeus's criterion of free-standing clauses and Tov's quantitative analysis of pluses/minuses both confirm moderate literalness.
dimensions.summary_plain: This translator usually follows the Hebrew word for word, but is willing to depart from strict literalness when meaning or tradition demands it.

examples.mt_text: נָבִיא מִקִּרְבְּךָ מֵאַחֶיךָ כָּמֹנִי יָקִים לְךָ יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֵלָיו תִּשְׁמָעוּן
examples.lxx_text: προφήτην ἐκ τῶν ἀδελφῶν σου ὡς ἐμὲ ἀναστήσει σοι κύριος ὁ θεός σου αὐτοῦ ἀκούσεσθε
examples.note: Near-isomorphic rendering; Hebrew syntactic order and lexical choices are preserved, demonstrating a default toward formal equivalence in narrative-legal material.

examples.mt_text: הַרְנִינוּ גֹויִם עַמֹּו כִּי דַם־עֲבָדָיו יִקֹּום
examples.lxx_text: εὐφράνθητε οὐρανοί ἅμα αὐτῷ καὶ προσκυνησάτωσαν αὐτῷ πάντες υἱοὶ θεοῦ
examples.note: The LXX preserves substantially more cola than the MT here, indicating either a fuller Vorlage (as confirmed by 4QDeutq) or expansionist tendencies in poetic contexts, reducing the apparent literalness score.

dimensions.summary: OG-Deut does not systematically reduce anthropomorphisms; indeed, compared to OG-Isaiah or the Targumim, theological smoothing is relatively rare in this book. Divine emotional vocabulary (e.g., אַף/θυμός, קִנְאָה/ζῆλος) is typically rendered literally throughout Deuteronomy. In the Song of Moses (ch. 32), the translator preserves vigorous divine action language (ἐκδικεῖ, ἀνταποδώσει) without euphemism. However, there are isolated cases elsewhere in Deuteronomy where יַד יְהוָה is rendered more abstractly, and 'mouth of the LORD' occasionally becomes 'word of the LORD,' suggesting mild but not systematic tendencies toward anthropomorphism reduction.
dimensions.summary_plain: This translator was not particularly bothered by descriptions of God acting with human-like body parts or emotions, and mostly translated them as-is.

examples.mt_text: כִּי דַם־עֲבָדָיו יִקֹּום וְנָקָם יָשִׁיב לְצָרָיו
examples.lxx_text: ὅτι τὸ αἷμα τῶν υἱῶν αὐτοῦ ἐκδικᾶται καὶ ἐκδικήσει καὶ ἀνταποδώσει δίκην τοῖς ἐχθροῖς
examples.note: Divine vengeance language is retained in full vigor without softening, indicating no theological anxiety about depicting God as an active avenger.

dimensions.summary: Deut 18:15 is the central test case: the rendering of כָּמֹנִי as ὡς ἐμέ is formally equivalent but the passage has demonstrably functioned in early Jewish and NT contexts as a messianic proof-text (Acts 3:22, 7:37), and the translator's choice not to disambiguate or deflate this potential is notable. The rendering does not actively heighten beyond the Hebrew, but neither does it suppress the typological resonance. In the Song of Moses, the addition of υἱοὶ θεοῦ and ἄγγελοι θεοῦ in 32:43 LXX enriches the cosmic-eschatological frame, which some scholars (Rösel, Dogniez) read as having eschatological implications. Overall the evidence for intentional messianic heightening is present but not dominant.
dimensions.summary_plain: The translator occasionally made choices that allowed passages to read with a messianic or end-times flavor, though this was probably not always intentional.

examples.mt_text: נָבִיא מִקִּרְבְּךָ מֵאַחֶיךָ כָּמֹנִי יָקִים לְךָ יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ
examples.lxx_text: προφήτην ἐκ τῶν ἀδελφῶν σου ὡς ἐμὲ ἀναστήσει σοι κύριος ὁ θεός σου
examples.note: The formally literal rendering nonetheless preserves the typological 'prophet like Moses' formulation that became a cornerstone of early messianic exegesis; the translator makes no move to generalize or de-singularize the promise.

examples.lxx_text: εὐφράνθητε οὐρανοί ἅμα αὐτῷ καὶ προσκυνησάτωσαν αὐτῷ πάντες υἱοὶ θεοῦ
examples.note: The expanded colon calling all 'sons of God' to worship introduces a cosmic liturgical dimension that heightens the eschatological grandeur of the divine vindication scene.

dimensions.summary: Harmonization is a well-documented feature of OG-Deut, particularly in legal material where Deuteronomy's laws parallel Exodus and Leviticus. The translator frequently aligns divergent formulations in Deuteronomy's law code with their parallels, a tendency documented extensively by Wevers and Tov. The Decalogue pericope (Deut 5) shows systematic harmonization toward the Exodus 20 version (e.g., additions of motivational clauses). In the sample passages, 32:8 LXX may reflect harmonization with a broader angelological tradition attested at Qumran (4QDeutj reads בְּנֵי אֱלֹהִים), and 32:43 LXX aligns more closely with the fuller Qumran text of the Song than the MT. While some divergences reflect a different Vorlage, the translator also actively smoothed intra-Deuteronomic repetitions.
dimensions.summary_plain: This translator had a noticeable habit of harmonizing Deuteronomy with parallel passages elsewhere in the Bible, making different texts agree with each other more than they do in Hebrew.

examples.mt_text: יַצֵּב גְּבֻלֹת עַמִּים לְמִסְפַּר בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
examples.lxx_text: ἔστησεν ὅρια ἐθνῶν κατὰ ἀριθμὸν ἀγγέλων θεοῦ
examples.note: The reading ἀγγέλων θεοῦ in place of MT's בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל aligns with an angelological Vorlage witnessed at Qumran and harmonizes with the broader ancient Near Eastern divine-council tradition; whether Vorlage or interpretive, it reflects ideological alignment with a coherent theological worldview.

dimensions.summary: OG-Deut is not predominantly a paraphrastic translation; Wevers's critical edition and Aejmelaeus's syntactic studies confirm that it generally reproduces Hebrew clause structure and lexical choices. However, in poetic passages (especially the Song of Moses, ch. 32, and the Blessing of Moses, ch. 33), the translator moves toward greater freedom, partly due to the difficulty of Hebrew poetry and partly due to a different textual tradition. The expansion in 32:43 LXX (with the two additional bicola absent from MT but attested at Qumran) significantly inflates the apparent paraphrase rate if one uses MT as the sole comparandum. Measured against likely Vorlage, the rate of genuine paraphrase is moderate, concentrated in poetry and rhetoric rather than law.
dimensions.summary_plain: The translator mostly stuck close to the Hebrew in the law sections, but became freer and more expansive when dealing with poetry and songs.

examples.mt_text: הַרְנִינוּ גֹויִם עַמֹּו כִּי דַם־עֲבָדָיו יִקֹּום וְנָקָם יָשִׁיב לְצָרָיו וְכִפֶּר אַדְמָתֹו עַמֹּו
examples.lxx_text: εὐφράνθητε οὐρανοί ἅμα αὐτῷ καὶ προσκυνησάτωσαν αὐτῷ πάντες υἱοὶ θεοῦ εὐφράνθητε ἔθνη μετὰ τοῦ λαοῦ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐνισχυσάτωσαν αὐτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι θεοῦ ὅτι τὸ αἷμα τῶν υἱῶν αὐτοῦ ἐκδικᾶται καὶ ἐκδικήσει καὶ ἀνταποδώσει δίκην τοῖς ἐχθροῖς καὶ τοῖς μισοῦσιν ἀνταποδώσει καὶ ἐκκαθαριεῖ κύριος τὴν γῆν τοῦ λαοῦ αὐτοῦ
examples.note: The LXX text is roughly twice the length of the MT here; the additions parallel 4QDeutq, suggesting the expansion derives at least partly from a fuller Vorlage, which complicates a simple verdict of paraphrase.

overall_assessment: The Old Greek of Deuteronomy presents a moderately literal translation with a consistent default toward formal equivalence in legal-didactic material, punctuated by greater freedom in poetic sections where both textual plurality and interpretive tradition played a role. Its most distinctive feature from a text-critical standpoint is not paraphrase per se but rather the witness to a Hebrew Vorlage that differed significantly from the proto-MT, particularly in the Song of Moses (ch. 32), where Qumran manuscripts (4QDeutj, 4QDeutq) corroborate LXX pluses. This makes OG-Deut an invaluable witness to pre-MT textual plurality, a finding central to Tov's text-critical methodology. In terms of Aejmelaeus's literary-analytical framework, the translator is best classified alongside OG-Numbers—moderately literal, with harmonizing tendencies concentrated in the law code and expanded cosmic-eschatological framing in poetry—and distinctly less free than OG-Isaiah or OG-Job.
overall_plain: The person who translated Deuteronomy into Greek was generally careful and close to the Hebrew, especially in legal sections, but was working with a Hebrew text that was sometimes different from what we know today—and those differences, especially in the poetic chapters, account for much of what looks like expansion or paraphrase. Comparing LXX Deuteronomy carefully with Dead Sea Scrolls texts has confirmed this again and again.

bibcrit_assessment.title: OG-Deut: Vorlage divergence, not translator freedom
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The single most significant insight about OG-Deut is that apparent deviations from MT—especially in the Song of Moses—are frequently explained by textual plurality at the pre-translation stage rather than by the translator's own theological or stylistic agenda. The Qumran evidence for a fuller text of Deut 32 (4QDeutj and 4QDeutq) means that what earlier scholarship classified as LXX expansions should be reclassified as evidence for a genuinely variant Hebrew Vorlage, fundamentally affecting how we evaluate this translator's 'paraphrase rate' and 'messianic heightening.'
bibcrit_assessment.plain: Many of the places where the Greek Deuteronomy looks different from the Hebrew Bible are actually because the translator was working from a different version of the Hebrew, not because they were adding or changing things themselves. The Dead Sea Scrolls proved this for several key passages.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis is broadly sound and reflects mainstream scholarship on OG-Deuteronomy, but contains a few specific Qumran manuscript attributions and textual claims that are imprecise or potentially incorrect.

flagged_claims.claim: 32:8 LXX may reflect harmonization with a broader angelological tradition attested at Qumran (4QDeutj reads בְּנֵי אֱלֹהִים)
flagged_claims.reason: The Qumran reading at Deut 32:8 supporting 'sons of God/El' is in 4QDeutj, but the actual reading is typically cited as בני אלוהים or בני אל—scholarly consensus leans toward בני אלוהים, but the specific reconstruction should be verified. More importantly, calling this 'harmonization with a broader angelological tradition' conflicts with the analysis's own later (correct) claim that this likely reflects a genuine variant Vorlage, not translator harmonization.

flagged_claims.claim: 32:43 LXX (with the two additional bicola absent from MT but attested at Qumran)
flagged_claims.reason: 4QDeutq's Hebrew text of 32:43 partially but not fully aligns with the LXX pluses. The LXX has roughly four added cola; 4QDeutq attests some but not all of these. The claim of 'two additional bicola' oversimplifies the complex relationship between 4QDeutq, LXX, and MT.

flagged_claims.claim: The Decalogue pericope (Deut 5) shows systematic harmonization toward the Exodus 20 version (e.g., additions of motivational clauses)
flagged_claims.reason: Harmonization in the Decalogue runs in both directions in the textual tradition (Exodus harmonized to Deut and vice versa, depending on textual witness). The claim that OG-Deut 5 systematically harmonizes toward Exodus 20 is overstated and would need specific examples; some harmonization runs the opposite direction.

flagged_claims.claim: best classified alongside OG-Numbers—moderately literal, with harmonizing tendencies
flagged_claims.reason: The pairing of OG-Deut with OG-Numbers as stylistic kin is plausible but not a standard taxonomic claim in the field; Wevers and others typically discuss the Greek Pentateuch translators with more nuance regarding shared vs. distinct profiles.

flagged_claims.claim: lxx_text of Deut 18:15 cited as 'προφήτην ἐκ τῶν ἀδελφῶν σου'
flagged_claims.reason: The Göttingen LXX (Wevers) of Deut 18:15 reads 'προφήτην ἐκ τῶν ἀδελφῶν σου ὡς ἐμὲ ἀναστήσει σοι κύριος ὁ θεός σου, αὐτοῦ ἀκούσεσθε'—but the analysis omits 'מקרבך' (ἐκ σοῦ / ἐκ μέσου σου) from the Greek while keeping it in the MT citation. The claim of near-isomorphism is then slightly undermined by the omission shown in the cited Greek.

safe_claims: OG-Deut occupies a middle position between very literal and very free translations
The Song of Moses (Deut 32) shows greater translation freedom and more textual divergence from MT than the legal sections
Deut 32:8 LXX reads ἀγγέλων θεοῦ where MT has בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
Deut 32:43 LXX is substantially longer than MT and has partial support from Qumran (4QDeutq)
Deut 18:15 functions as a messianic proof-text in Acts 3:22 and 7:37
Vorlage divergence rather than translator freedom accounts for many MT-LXX differences in Deut 32
Wevers's Göttingen edition and Aejmelaeus's syntactic studies are foundational for OG-Deut analysis
